14: # Create Skill Router
15: 
16: The machine router for [`SKILL.md`](./SKILL.md). `SKILL.md` keeps the short routing prose and the
17: link that points here; this file holds the declaration a reader parses to decide what loads.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: The router answers one question: given a request, which skill-local resources load, in what order, and
24: what happens when nothing matches. Every path below stays inside this skill folder, and no resource
25: loads before an intent selects it.
26: 
27: Requests reach this packet when they ask to create or rebuild an OpenCode skill under `.skilled/skills/`, to run `/create:skill` for a standalone skill or `/create:skill-parent` for a parent hub, to author or repair a skill package's `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/`, `scripts/` or `changelog/`, or to validate and package a skill with `scripts/package_skill.py`. Its vocabulary is `create skill`, `new skill`, `skill scaffold`, `SKILL.md scaffold`, `OpenCode skill`, `parent hub`, `mode packet`, `nested workflow packet` and `package skill`. It routes to two resource families: the `references/shared/` doctrine and its root-metadata contract, which both modes load first, and the mode's own `references/<key>/` plus `assets/<key>/` trees, where `create-skill` resolves the `skill` key and `create-skill-parent` resolves `parent-skill`.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. INTENT MODEL
32: 
33: - **`SKILL_PACKAGE`** fires on `create skill`, `/create:skill`, `new skill`, `skill scaffold`, `SKILL.md scaffold`, `OpenCode skill`, `sk-skill`, `create sk-`, `reusable capability`, `reusable helper`, `starter reference docs` and `package skill` at weight 4. It loads the five shared docs — `references/shared/overview.md`, `references/shared/common-pitfalls.md`, `references/shared/validation-and-packaging.md`, `references/shared/advisor-index-handoff.md`, `references/shared/skill-root-metadata-contract.md` — then `references/skill/creation-workflow.md`, `references/skill/examples-and-maintenance.md`, `references/skill/upgrading-a-skill-to-v4.md`, and the nine `assets/skill/` templates: `assets/skill/skill-md-template.md`, `assets/skill/skill-readme-template.md`, `assets/skill/skill-reference-template.md`, `assets/skill/skill-asset-template.md`, `assets/skill/skill-procedure-template.md`, `assets/skill/skill-scaffold-template.md`, `assets/skill/skill-smart-router.md`, `assets/skill/skill-router-template.md`, `assets/skill/skill-sync-manifest-template.md`.
34: - **`PARENT_HUB`** fires on `/create:skill-parent`, `parent skill`, `parent hub`, `mode packet`, `nested workflow packet`, `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` at weight 4. It loads the same five shared docs, then `references/parent-skill/parent-skills-nested-packets.md`, `references/parent-skill/parent-hub-router-schema.md`, `references/parent-skill/compiled-routing-architecture.md`, and the five `assets/parent-skill/` templates: `assets/parent-skill/parent-skill-hub-template.md`, `assets/parent-skill/parent-skill-readme-template.md`, `assets/parent-skill/parent-skill-root-router-template.md`, `assets/parent-skill/scaffold/hub-skill-scaffold.md`, `assets/parent-skill/scaffold/packet-skill-scaffold.md`.
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 3. MACHINE ROUTER
39: 
40: The one machine-readable projection of the intent model above, written as `## MACHINE ROUTER` so every
41: reader finds it. This section is the last in the file, and it holds the only pseudocode.
42: 
43: This section holds the packet's mode tree, its route selection, the resource domains it loads and the smart-router pseudocode that reads them.
44:

46:

48: SKILL AUTHORING REQUEST
49:     |
50:     +- Standalone skill -> workflowMode: sk-create-skill
51:     |   +- scripts/init_skill.py
52:     |   +- assets/skill/skill-md-template.md

57:         +- assets/parent-skill/parent-skill-hub-template.md
58:         +- assets/parent-skill/parent-skill-registry-template.json
59:         +- assets/parent-skill/parent-skill-hub-router-template.json
60: ```

15: # Advisor Index Handoff
16: 
17: The shared field vocabulary that `/create:skill`, `/create:skill-parent`, `/doctor:skill-advisor tune`, and `/doctor:skill-advisor parent-skill` all render after touching a skill root, so that scaffolding a skill and diagnosing its advisor state describe the same reality in the same words.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: **When to Use**:
24: - Wiring a create or doctor workflow asset's completion/report section (A5 in `002-core-alignment-fixes/plan.md`)
25: - Writing a contract test that pins the shared vocabulary across adapters (A6)
26: - Deciding whether a given create branch renders the full handoff or the narrow leaf-freshness signal only (§6)
27: 
28: **Core Principle**: One vocabulary, not one formatter. Create and doctor are separate prompt-asset workflows with genuinely different result shapes (create reports a scaffold; doctor reports a mutating, phase-gated diagnostic run) — see `research.md` Theme F1/F2 in `035-create-doctor-skill-advisor-alignment/001-research/`. What must stay identical across both is the field names, the metadata-ownership statements, and the verification-state enum below, not the surrounding prose or layout.
29: 
30: > **Advisor refresh is always operator-owned.** No `/create:*` or `/doctor:*` workflow calls `skill_graph_scan` or `advisor_rebuild` as a side effect of scaffolding or diagnosing a skill. Every workflow that touches a skill root reports refresh status as `NOT RUN` and prints the exact command the operator would run — never chains it automatically (research.md Theme B1/B7, "Questions Answered").
31: >
32: > The one deliberate rebuild is `/doctor:skill-advisor rebuild`. The operator invokes it to run `advisor_rebuild` and then `skill_graph_scan` behind a backup of `skill-graph.sqlite`. It does not touch a skill root and does not render the handoff below.
33: 
34: ---
35: 
36: ## 2. METADATA OWNERSHIP
37: 
38: Four files carry advisor-relevant metadata on a skill root. Each has exactly one producer; none is validated against another's vocabulary.
39: 
40: | File | Producer | What it is | Advisor relevance |
41: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
42: | `description.json` | authored | Descriptive hub-doctor metadata | **None.** Not discovered or validated by the graph compiler. Never becomes advisor input, and never validated against graph vocabulary — see §5 Guardrail. |
43: | `graph-metadata.json` | authored | Sole hub advisor identity | The only file `skill_graph_scan` discovers and `skill_graph_validate` checks. |
44: | `leaf-manifest.json` | **generated** | Leaf/resource projection derived from the registry and packet corpus | Never hand-edited. State is `fresh`, `stale`, or `missing` — see §4. |
45: | `command-metadata.json` | authored, H-only, optional | Slash-command-to-mode binding | Present and validated when the hub owns commands; omitted (not empty) when it owns none. |
46: 
47: Full generated-versus-authored rules and the H/S class matrix live in `skill-root-metadata-contract.md` in this same directory — this document only states the subset relevant to the create → advisor handoff.
48: 
49: ---
50: 
51: ## 3. REFRESH OWNERSHIP
52: 
53: Refresh is a deliberate, explicit operator choice between two non-equivalent paths — never an unconditional chain, because `advisor_rebuild` already calls the same metadata indexer internally before publishing its own generation (research.md Theme B7).
54: 
55: ```bash
56: cd "<selected_repo>"
57: 
58: # Full advisor refresh (rebuild + republish)
59: node .skilled/bin/skill-advisor.cjs advisor_rebuild --trusted --workspace-root "$PWD" --force true --format json
60: 
61: # Graph-only refresh (scan without republishing the advisor)
62: node .skilled/bin/skill-advisor.cjs skill_graph_scan --trusted --skills-root "$PWD/.skilled/skills" --format json
63: ```
64: 
65: Verification, run after either refresh path (or on its own to diagnose current state):
66: 
67: ```bash
68: node .skilled/bin/skill-advisor.cjs skill_graph_validate --format json
69: node .skilled/bin/skill-advisor.cjs advisor_status --workspace-root "$PWD" --format json
70: ```
71: 
72: `skill_graph_scan` resolves `process.cwd()` as workspace root and rejects paths outside it — the `cd` is load-bearing, not decorative, when the operator is working from a linked worktree (research.md Theme B6).
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 4. VERIFICATION-STATE VOCABULARY
77: 
78: Every refresh or validation field a create/doctor workflow renders uses exactly one of these four states:
79: 
80: | State | Meaning |
81: | --- | --- |
82: | `NOT RUN` | Operator-owned action was not taken by this workflow (the default for every create-time refresh field). |
83: | `PASSED` | The action ran and its result was clean. |
84: | `FAILED` | The action ran and found a real problem (structural graph error, failed test, generation error). |
85: | `UNAVAILABLE (retryable)` | The call threw, returned a non-ok status, or the payload was malformed — typically the advisor IPC socket being cold (exit 75). Never render this as `FAILED`; it is a transport state, not a finding. |
86: 
87: `leaf-manifest.json` freshness uses its own three-value state, not the four above, because it describes a generated file's currency rather than a pass/fail check:
88: 
89: | State | Meaning |
90: | --- | --- |
91: | `fresh` | Generated after the current registry/packet corpus; content matches what `generate-leaf-manifest.cjs --write` would produce now. |
92: | `stale` | Present but predates a later registry/packet change. |
93: | `missing` | Not present on disk. |
94: 
95: Doctor severity derivation for `skill_graph_validate` (`pass`/`warn`/`fail`/`unavailable`) and the workflow-level terminal states (`fail`/`partial`/`pass`/`skipped_unverified`) are doctor-specific compositions of this vocabulary, not additional enums — see `doctor-skill-advisor-tune.yaml`'s `phase_4_verify` for the full derivation.
96: 
97: ---
98: 
99: ## 5. CLASS APPLICABILITY
100: 
101: H-only fields render **omitted**, not `N/A` or a false negative, on standalone (class-S) roots — `description.json`, `mode-registry.json`, `hub-router.json`, and `command-metadata.json` are structurally forbidden there (`skill-root-metadata-contract.md` §3). A standalone `/create:skill` result that reported `description.json: MISSING` would be wrong; it should not mention the field at all.
102: 
103: **Guardrail (do not build this):** `description.json` stays descriptive and is never validated against graph vocabulary, and standalone `/create:skill` never asserts parent-hub metadata files. This boundary was raised and re-confirmed across nine iterations of research (Theme C, research.md) specifically because it is the mistake future maintainers are most likely to reintroduce — resist adding a `description.json` ↔ `graph-metadata.json` equality check or a parent-file requirement to a standalone assertion, however tempting it looks as a "consistency" improvement.
104: 
105: ---
106: 
107: ## 6. BRANCH SCOPE — WHO RENDERS WHAT
108: 
109: | Branch | Renders |
110: | --- | --- |
111: | Standalone `/create:skill` full-create | Full handoff, `standalone` scope (H-only fields omitted) |
112: | Standalone `/create:skill` full-update | Full handoff, `standalone` scope |
113: | Parent `/create:skill-parent` create | Full handoff, H-specific values (`leaf-manifest.json` freshness from the scoped generator this workflow just ran) |
114: | Parent `/create:skill-parent` update | Full handoff, H-specific values |
115: | Reference-only / asset-only create branches | **Not** the full handoff — only the narrow conditional `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/generate-leaf-manifest.cjs --check <skillDir>` leaf-freshness signal, gated on the changed path falling under a configured leaf root |
116: | `/doctor:skill-advisor tune` | Full handoff vocabulary, live values from `skill_graph_validate`/`advisor_rebuild`/`advisor_validate` |
117: | `/doctor:skill-advisor parent-skill` | Full handoff vocabulary, read-only. Distinguishes `leaf-manifest.json` missing from stale and points at the scoped generator, never attempts repair |
118: 
119: Rendering the full handoff on a reference/asset-only branch would be misleading: those branches touch roots where the H-only fields are forbidden, so most of the handoff would be inapplicable noise around one real signal (research.md Theme F7).

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
23: 
24: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
25: 
26: **Core Purpose**:
27: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
28: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
29: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
30: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
31: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
32: 
33: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
34: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
35: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
36: 
37: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
38: 
39: ```
40: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
41:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
42:             ↓
43: Level 2: SKILL.md body
44:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
45:             ↓
46: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
47:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
48: ```
49: 
50: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
51: 
52: ### Location & Naming
53: 
54: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
55: 
56: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
57: 
58: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
59: |---------------|-----------------|
60: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
61: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
62: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
63: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
64: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
65: 
66: ---
67: 
68: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
69: 
70: ### Title and Intro
71: 
72: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
73: 
74: ```markdown
75: ---
76: title: [Title]
77: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
78: trigger_phrases:
79:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
80:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
81:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
82: importance_tier: normal
83: contextType: general
84: version: 1.0.0.0
85: ---
86: 
87: # [Title]
88: 
89: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: \## 1. OVERVIEW
94: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
95: 
96: ```
97: 
98: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block. The Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal:
99: - 3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content
100: - `importance_tier`, which defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs
101: - `contextType`, one of `planning|research|implementation|general`
102: 
103: See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
104: 
105: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
106: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
107: 
108: #### GOOD Intro Structure
109: 
110: ```markdown
111: # Git Commit Workflows
112: 
113: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
114: 
115: ---
116: 
117: \## 1. OVERVIEW
118: 
119: ### Purpose
120: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
121: 
122: ### When to Use
123: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
124: - Filtering generated files from commits
125: - Writing clear commit messages
126: 
127: ### Core Principle
128: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
129: ```
130: 
131: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
132: 
133: ```markdown
134: # Git Commit Workflows
135: 
136: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
137: 
138: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
139: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
140:

1: ---
2: title: "create-skill"
3: description: "Scaffold, validate and package standalone OpenCode skills and two-axis parent hubs from vetted templates, for anyone building or repairing a skill under .skilled/skills/."
4: trigger_phrases:
5:   - "create skill"
6:   - "parent hub"
7: version: 1.2.5.0
8: ---
9: 
10: # create-skill
11: 
12: > You get a validated skill or parent hub scaffolded from vetted templates, with routing and metadata already proven, not a blank file and a guess.
13: 
14: ---
15: 
16: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
17: 
18: | Aspect | What you get |
19: |---|---|
20: | **Use it for** | Scaffolding, validating and packaging OpenCode skills under `.skilled/skills/`, standalone or parent hub |
21: | **Invoke with** | `/create:skill`, `/create:skill-parent`, "new skill", "parent hub" |
22: | **Works on** | New skill folders and existing skill or hub packages that need repair or re-validation |
23: | **Produces** | `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` for a skill, a full parent-hub router set for a hub |
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. OVERVIEW
28: 
29: ### What It Does
30: 
31: create-skill runs one of two workflow modes from a single packet. `create-skill` scaffolds a standalone skill with its own advisor identity, `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/`, built with `scripts/init_skill.py` and normalized to this repo's section order. `create-skill-parent` scaffolds a parent hub that dispatches to nested workflow or surface packets, with `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` at the hub root and `graph-metadata.json` only there, never inside a nested packet. Both modes end at the same gate: `scripts/validate_skill_package.py` must exit clean before `scripts/package_skill.py` runs. It does not audit or improve an existing skill's prose quality once the skill already exists and only needs review. That is `create-quality-control`.
32: 
33: ### Why This Skill Exists
34: 
35: Hand-rolling a new skill from a blank `SKILL.md` means reinventing frontmatter rules, section order, routing pseudocode and validation gates every single time. The drift shows up as skills that skip a required field, use the wrong version format, bury routing logic where the advisor can never find it or miss a validation gate entirely. A parent hub multiplies that risk across a registry, a router and however many nested packets, all of which have to agree with each other or the hub silently misroutes. create-skill exists to scaffold both shapes from vetted templates and then prove the result is valid before anyone calls it done.
36: 
37: ### The Two Workflow Modes
38: 
39: | Mode | What the skill scaffolds |
40: |---|---|
41: | **`create-skill`** | a standalone skill folder with its own advisor identity, `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` |
42: | **`create-skill-parent`** | a parent hub root with `mode-registry.json`, `hub-router.json`, root `ROUTER.md` (`stage1-only` on a fresh scaffold), `description.json`, `graph-metadata.json` and `command-metadata.json`, plus a `SKILL.md`, `README.md` and `changelog/` per nested packet |
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 3. QUICK START
47: 
48: > Run these commands from the repository root.
49: 
50: **Step 1: Scaffold a standalone skill.**
51: 
52: ```bash
53: # --path is the PARENT directory. init_skill.py creates <path>/my-skill
54: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path .skilled/skills
55: ```
56: 
57: `init_skill.py` creates `my-skill/` with `SKILL.md`, `ROUTER.md` and two prepared trees: a `manual-testing-playbook/` corpus index and a `benchmark/reports/` tree carrying its own run index. `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` are added by hand as the skill earns them.
58: 
59: **Step 2: Fill in the real content, then validate.**
60: 
61: ```bash
62: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/validate_skill_package.py .skilled/skills/<skill-name>
63: ```
64: 
65: Expected output ends with `package_skill.py --check: PASS (exit 0)`.
66: 
67: **Step 3: Package only after validation passes.**
68: 
69: ```bash
70: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/package_skill.py .skilled/skills/<skill-name> <output-directory>
71: ```
72: 
73: Expected: ✅ Successfully packaged <file-count> files to: <output-directory>/<skill-name>.zip
74: 
75: ---
76: 
77: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
78: 
79: ### The Standalone Path
80: 
81: The standalone path starts with concrete examples of what the skill needs to do, then clarifies purpose, trigger phrases, output contract and boundaries before any file gets written. From there each piece of reusable content gets a home: deterministic or repeatedly-rewritten code goes in `scripts/`, domain knowledge and detailed workflow guidance goes in `references/` and templates or output resources go in `assets/`. `scripts/init_skill.py` scaffolds the folder. Generated files get normalized to the repo's section order and trimmed of anything unneeded, then `SKILL.md` gets authored as an executable contract with `WHEN TO USE`, `SMART ROUTING`, `HOW IT WORKS`, `RULES` and `SUCCESS CRITERIA`. Validation runs before any completion claim. Packaging only runs after validation passes.
82: 
83: ### The Parent-Hub Path
84: 
85: The parent-hub path starts by confirming the target really is one advisor-routable identity, not several skills that happen to be related. `scripts/init_skill.py --kind parent` then scaffolds the hub root (`SKILL.md`, `mode-registry.json`, `hub-router.json`, root `ROUTER.md` with `router_state: stage1-only`, `description.json`, `graph-metadata.json`, `command-metadata.json` and the generated `leaf-manifest.json`) and each nested packet gets its own `SKILL.md`, `README.md` and `changelog/`, with no packet-local `graph-metadata.json` anywhere but the root. The root `ROUTER.md` stays `stage1-only` (empty maps, all routing in stage one) until an author promotes it to `active` with a concrete, resolvable leaf map. The scaffolder never fabricates placeholder intents.
86: 
87: ### Compiled Routing: Legacy Versus Ready
88: 
89: `--compiled-routing legacy` and `--compiled-routing ready` produce genuinely different on-disk artifacts for the same hub shape. The authoring workflow asks which one you want rather than silently picking. Legacy leaves the router directive in place with no canonical manifest, which is backward compatible with every existing call. Ready mints a canonical manifest with `compiled-route-manifest.cjs mint`, then verifies it is fresh and only reports `compiled-ready` when both steps succeed. A failed mint or a stale manifest falls back to legacy rather than ever hand-authoring a manifest or a digest. Either way, a ready manifest stays inert onboarding evidence: it never activates compiled serving or changes the repository default on its own.
90: 
91: ### Replaying Stage-Two Leaf Routes
92: 
93: When a hub's `ROUTER.md` keyword block scores a request, the winning intents pick the leaf routes. [`scripts/leaf-route-replay.cjs`](./scripts/leaf-route-replay.cjs) measures how well those picks match the committed gold scenarios. With no switch it makes no model call. It scores each hub's predicted leaf routes against the gold routes and prints one `hub=` line per hub plus a `total` line. `--transcripts <dir>` counts real `ROUTER.md` reads in a folder you name without printing any text. `--prose <file>` compares the keyword arm against a prose arm and prints one `replay verdict:` line that keeps, drops or stops.
94: 
95: ```bash
96: node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/leaf-route-replay.cjs --report <dir> --transcripts <dir> --prose <file>
97: ```
98: 
99: ---
100: 
101: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
102:

13: 
14: ---

16: ## 1. AT A GLANCE

18: | Aspect | What you get |

21: | **Invoke with** | `/create:skill`, `/create:skill-parent`, "new skill", "parent hub" |
22: | **Works on** | New skill folders and existing skill or hub packages that need repair or re-validation |

24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. OVERVIEW
28: 
29: ### What It Does
30: 
31: create-skill runs one of two workflow modes from a single packet. `create-skill` scaffolds a standalone skill with its own advisor identity, `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/`, built with `scripts/init_skill.py` and normalized to this repo's section order. `create-skill-parent` scaffolds a parent hub that dispatches to nested workflow or surface packets, with `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` at the hub root and `graph-metadata.json` only there, never inside a nested packet. Both modes end at the same gate: `scripts/validate_skill_package.py` must exit clean before `scripts/package_skill.py` runs. It does not audit or improve an existing skill's prose quality once the skill already exists and only needs review. That is `create-quality-control`.
32: 
33: ### Why This Skill Exists
34: 
35: Hand-rolling a new skill from a blank `SKILL.md` means reinventing frontmatter rules, section order, routing pseudocode and validation gates every single time. The drift shows up as skills that skip a required field, use the wrong version format, bury routing logic where the advisor can never find it or miss a validation gate entirely. A parent hub multiplies that risk across a registry, a router and however many nested packets, all of which have to agree with each other or the hub silently misroutes. create-skill exists to scaffold both shapes from vetted templates and then prove the result is valid before anyone calls it done.
36: 
37: ### The Two Workflow Modes
38: 
39: | Mode | What the skill scaffolds |
40: |---|---|
41: | **`create-skill`** | a standalone skill folder with its own advisor identity, `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` |
42: | **`create-skill-parent`** | a parent hub root with `mode-registry.json`, `hub-router.json`, root `ROUTER.md` (`stage1-only` on a fresh scaffold), `description.json`, `graph-metadata.json` and `command-metadata.json`, plus a `SKILL.md`, `README.md` and `changelog/` per nested packet |
43: 
44: ---

46: ## 3. QUICK START
47: 
48: > Run these commands from the repository root.
49: 
50: **Step 1: Scaffold a standalone skill.**
51: 
52: ```bash
53: # --path is the PARENT directory. init_skill.py creates <path>/my-skill
54: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path .skilled/skills
55: ```
56: 
57: `init_skill.py` creates `my-skill/` with `SKILL.md`, `ROUTER.md` and two prepared trees: a `manual-testing-playbook/` corpus index and a `benchmark/reports/` tree carrying its own run index. `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` are added by hand as the skill earns them.
58: 
59: **Step 2: Fill in the real content, then validate.**
60: 
61: ```bash
62: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/validate_skill_package.py .skilled/skills/<skill-name>
63: ```
64: 
65: Expected output ends with `package_skill.py --check: PASS (exit 0)`.
66: 
67: **Step 3: Package only after validation passes.**
68:

70: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/package_skill.py .skilled/skills/<skill-name> <output-directory>
71: ```
72: 
73: Expected: ✅ Successfully packaged <file-count> files to: <output-directory>/<skill-name>.zip
74:

77: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
78: 
79: ### The Standalone Path
80: 
81: The standalone path starts with concrete examples of what the skill needs to do, then clarifies purpose, trigger phrases, output contract and boundaries before any file gets written. From there each piece of reusable content gets a home: deterministic or repeatedly-rewritten code goes in `scripts/`, domain knowledge and detailed workflow guidance goes in `references/` and templates or output resources go in `assets/`. `scripts/init_skill.py` scaffolds the folder. Generated files get normalized to the repo's section order and trimmed of anything unneeded, then `SKILL.md` gets authored as an executable contract with `WHEN TO USE`, `SMART ROUTING`, `HOW IT WORKS`, `RULES` and `SUCCESS CRITERIA`. Validation runs before any completion claim. Packaging only runs after validation passes.
82: 
83: ### The Parent-Hub Path
84: 
85: The parent-hub path starts by confirming the target really is one advisor-routable identity, not several skills that happen to be related. `scripts/init_skill.py --kind parent` then scaffolds the hub root (`SKILL.md`, `mode-registry.json`, `hub-router.json`, root `ROUTER.md` with `router_state: stage1-only`, `description.json`, `graph-metadata.json`, `command-metadata.json` and the generated `leaf-manifest.json`) and each nested packet gets its own `SKILL.md`, `README.md` and `changelog/`, with no packet-local `graph-metadata.json` anywhere but the root. The root `ROUTER.md` stays `stage1-only` (empty maps, all routing in stage one) until an author promotes it to `active` with a concrete, resolvable leaf map. The scaffolder never fabricates placeholder intents.
86: 
87: ### Compiled Routing: Legacy Versus Ready
88: 
89: `--compiled-routing legacy` and `--compiled-routing ready` produce genuinely different on-disk artifacts for the same hub shape. The authoring workflow asks which one you want rather than silently picking. Legacy leaves the router directive in place with no canonical manifest, which is backward compatible with every existing call. Ready mints a canonical manifest with `compiled-route-manifest.cjs mint`, then verifies it is fresh and only reports `compiled-ready` when both steps succeed. A failed mint or a stale manifest falls back to legacy rather than ever hand-authoring a manifest or a digest. Either way, a ready manifest stays inert onboarding evidence: it never activates compiled serving or changes the repository default on its own.
90: 
91: ### Replaying Stage-Two Leaf Routes
92: 
93: When a hub's `ROUTER.md` keyword block scores a request, the winning intents pick the leaf routes. [`scripts/leaf-route-replay.cjs`](./scripts/leaf-route-replay.cjs) measures how well those picks match the committed gold scenarios. With no switch it makes no model call. It scores each hub's predicted leaf routes against the gold routes and prints one `hub=` line per hub plus a `total` line. `--transcripts <dir>` counts real `ROUTER.md` reads in a folder you name without printing any text. `--prose <file>` compares the keyword arm against a prose arm and prints one `replay verdict:` line that keeps, drops or stops.
94: 
95: ```bash
96: node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/leaf-route-replay.cjs --report <dir> --transcripts <dir> --prose <file>
97: ```

20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: A skill root carries up to nine metadata JSON files. Which of them apply is not a per-skill preference: it follows from the root's **class**, and the class follows from one authored declaration.
23: 
24: **When to Use**:
25: - Creating a new skill or parent hub and deciding which metadata files to write
26: - Auditing an existing root, or diagnosing a `ci-skill-root-metadata` failure
27: - Deciding whether a metadata file may be generated or must be authored
28: 
29: **Core Principle**: Classify first, then check. A root's class is decided by an authored declaration, never by a generated artifact.
30: 
31: > **Not the spec-folder schema.** `description.json` and `graph-metadata.json` also exist under `.opencode/specs/` under a completely separate continuity schema. The two are never the same file and never interchangeable. This contract governs `.skilled/skills/<root>/` only, and the gate never scans the spec tree.
32: 
33: ---
34: 
35: ## 2. THE TWO CLASSES
36: 
37: | Class | What it is | Discriminator |
38: | --- | --- | --- |
39: | **H** — packet hub | Routes prompts across several mode packets and projects one advisor identity | Declares **both** `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` |
40: | **S** — standalone routed-resource skill | One workflow mode; its `references/`, `assets/`, `feature-catalog/`, `hooks/` and `manual-testing-playbook/` docs are the routed corpus | Declares **neither** |
41: 
42: The registry and the router are the discriminator because they are consumed as one coupled declaration — the router's signal keys must name registry modes. A root carrying exactly one of them is therefore not a third class; it is a half-written declaration, and the gate rejects it rather than guessing.
43: 
44: Classification deliberately ignores every other file, including generated output. If a generated manifest could change a root's class, then a root whose manifest was never written would classify differently after regeneration, and the gate could never report that manifest as missing.
45: 
46: `ROUTER.md` is deliberately outside classification. The root `ROUTER.md` stage-two control document is a markdown companion, not a JSON metadata file: it never appears in the required/forbidden/generated sets below, it never changes a root's class, and a hub is classified by `mode-registry.json` plus `hub-router.json` whether or not it carries a root router. `ROUTER.md` is also never a leaf, advisor identity, or typed leaf-manifest pair — it is enforced by the separate root-router contract validator, not by this metadata gate.
47:

60: **Folder Organization Principle**:
61: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills
62:   - Grouped example: `references/core-standards.md`, `references/validation.md`
63:   - Domain example: `references/backend/go/`, `references/frontend/react/`
64: - **assets/** = Subfolders ALLOWED when organizing many files by category
65:   - Group related templates together for clarity
66:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
67: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections
68: 
69: ### SKILL.md Requirements
70: 
71: **Metadata Quality**: The `name` and `description` in YAML frontmatter determine when the AI agent will use the skill. Be specific about what the skill does and when to use it.
72: 
73: **Writing Style Guidelines**:
74: - Use **third-person** in descriptions (e.g., "This skill should be used when..." instead of "Use this skill when...")
75: - Write using **imperative/infinitive form** (verb-first instructions), not second person
76: - Use objective, instructional language (e.g., "To accomplish X, do Y" rather than "You should do X")
77: - Keep SKILL.md body under **5k words**
78: 
79: **Required Sections** (enforced by markdown-document-specialist validation):
80: 1. WHEN TO USE (activation triggers and use cases ONLY)
81: 2. SMART ROUTING (8 to 12 lines of plain prose: what selects this skill, what it loads first, where the machine router is)
82: 3. HOW IT WORKS
83: 4. RULES (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
84: 5. REFERENCES (or combined `SMART ROUTING & REFERENCES`)
85: 
86: Validation reminder:
87: - `scripts/package_skill.py` fails if `REFERENCES` is missing and no approved combined heading variant is present.
88: 
89: **Recommended Sections**:
90: 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
91: 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
92: 8. RELATED RESOURCES
93: 
94: ### README.md Guidance
95: 
96: Create `README.md` when the skill needs human-facing orientation beyond runtime routing. Use [skill-readme-template.md](../../assets/skill/skill-readme-template.md) for skill package READMEs rather than the generic folder README template.
97: 
98: Include a skill README when:
99: - Operators need a quick start, examples, troubleshooting or FAQ.
100: - The skill has multiple modes, resource domains, scripts or validation commands.
101: - Readers need a concise map that explains how `SKILL.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` fit together.
102: 
103: Keep boundaries clear:
104: - `SKILL.md` is the runtime instruction and routing surface.
105: - `README.md` is the human orientation and navigation surface.
106: - Long conceptual depth belongs in focused `references/` files.
107: 
108: ### Routing Authority Standard
109: 
110: The machine router is the authoritative routing source. It sits in the sibling `ROUTER.md`, in a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` section that is the last H2 of that file. Section 2 of `SKILL.md` stays short prose that links to it. Do not maintain separate use-case routing tables.
111: 
112: Router parity checklist for the machine router block:
113: - Guarded in-skill loading (`_guard_in_skill`)
114: - Recursive markdown discovery (`discover_markdown_resources`)
115: - Weighted intent scoring (`score_intents`)
116: - Ambiguity handling (`select_intents`)

60: **Folder Organization Principle**:
61: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills

66:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
67: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections
68: 
69: ### SKILL.md Requirements
70: 
71: **Metadata Quality**: The `name` and `description` in YAML frontmatter determine when the AI agent will use the skill. Be specific about what the skill does and when to use it.
72: 
73: **Writing Style Guidelines**:
74: - Use **third-person** in descriptions (e.g., "This skill should be used when..." instead of "Use this skill when...")
75: - Write using **imperative/infinitive form** (verb-first instructions), not second person
76: - Use objective, instructional language (e.g., "To accomplish X, do Y" rather than "You should do X")
77: - Keep SKILL.md body under **5k words**
78: 
79: **Required Sections** (enforced by markdown-document-specialist validation):
80: 1. WHEN TO USE (activation triggers and use cases ONLY)
81: 2. SMART ROUTING (8 to 12 lines of plain prose: what selects this skill, what it loads first, where the machine router is)
82: 3. HOW IT WORKS
83: 4. RULES (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
84: 5. REFERENCES (or combined `SMART ROUTING & REFERENCES`)
85:

87: - `scripts/package_skill.py` fails if `REFERENCES` is missing and no approved combined heading variant is present.
88:

90: 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
91: 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
92: 8. RELATED RESOURCES

94: ### README.md Guidance
95: 
96: Create `README.md` when the skill needs human-facing orientation beyond runtime routing. Use [skill-readme-template.md](../../assets/skill/skill-readme-template.md) for skill package READMEs rather than the generic folder README template.

104: - `SKILL.md` is the runtime instruction and routing surface.

15: # Common Skill-Creation Pitfalls
16: 
17: The recurring mistakes that keep skills from triggering, bloat the context window, or fail packaging — each with a concrete before/after fix.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: This reference catalogs the nine pitfalls that most often degrade a skill: from descriptions that are too vague or too bloated to trigger reliably, through second-person voice and platform-specific assumptions, to YAML mistakes, section placement and a router in the wrong place. Each pitfall pairs a wrong example with the corrected form.
24: 
25: **When to Use**:
26: - A skill exists but does not trigger when expected
27: - SKILL.md is straining the context window
28: - Packaging or budget checks are failing
29: - Reviewing a freshly authored skill for common defects
30: 
31: **Core Principle**: Most failed skills fail at the description and the section boundaries — fix those first.
32: 
33: > **Note on examples below**: illustrative SKILL.md headings inside the fenced examples are written `\##` (not `##`) so the section-numbering validator — which scans `## N.` lines regardless of code fences — does not count them as this document's own sections. Drop the leading `\` when copying a heading into a real SKILL.md.
34: 
35: ---
36: 
37: ## 2. COMMON PITFALLS
38: 
39: ### Pitfall 1: Generic or Bloated Descriptions
40: 
41: **Problem**: Skill doesn't trigger because description is too vague — OR the project total exceeds Claude Code's 8,000-char `SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET` and the harness silently drops the skill from auto-discovery.
42: 
43: **Example — too generic**:
44: ```yaml
45: # Bad — vague, no routing keywords
46: description: Helps with markdown files
47: ```
48: 
49: **Example — too bloated** (real trim, 545 → 125 chars):
50: ```yaml
51: # Bad — enumerates stacks, lists libraries, marketing prose

15: # Common Skill-Creation Pitfalls
16: 
17: The recurring mistakes that keep skills from triggering, bloat the context window, or fail packaging — each with a concrete before/after fix.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: This reference catalogs the nine pitfalls that most often degrade a skill: from descriptions that are too vague or too bloated to trigger reliably, through second-person voice and platform-specific assumptions, to YAML mistakes, section placement and a router in the wrong place. Each pitfall pairs a wrong example with the corrected form.
24: 
25: **When to Use**:
26: - A skill exists but does not trigger when expected
27: - SKILL.md is straining the context window
28: - Packaging or budget checks are failing
29: - Reviewing a freshly authored skill for common defects
30: 
31: **Core Principle**: Most failed skills fail at the description and the section boundaries — fix those first.
32: 
33: > **Note on examples below**: illustrative SKILL.md headings inside the fenced examples are written `\##` (not `##`) so the section-numbering validator — which scans `## N.` lines regardless of code fences — does not count them as this document's own sections. Drop the leading `\` when copying a heading into a real SKILL.md.
34: 
35: ---
36: 
37: ## 2. COMMON PITFALLS
38: 
39: ### Pitfall 1: Generic or Bloated Descriptions
40: 
41: **Problem**: Skill doesn't trigger because description is too vague — OR the project total exceeds Claude Code's 8,000-char `SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET` and the harness silently drops the skill from auto-discovery.
42: 
43: **Example — too generic**:
44: ```yaml
45: # Bad — vague, no routing keywords
46: description: Helps with markdown files
47: ```
48:

51: # Bad — enumerates stacks, lists libraries, marketing prose

15: # Compiled-Routing Architecture For Parent Hubs
16: 
17: The compiled skill router is a closed-cohort, byte-verified fast path that resolves a parent hub's `workflowMode` decision without evaluating the hub's prose smart-router at request time. It exists for exactly the parent hubs that have built and proven a compiled policy against that hub's own legacy routing — no other skill, including any hub `create-skill` scaffolds today, is reachable through it.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: Two routers coexist for a parent hub:
24: 
25: - The **prose smart-router** — the hub's `SMART ROUTING` section plus its root `ROUTER.md`, read and reasoned over by the acting agent at request time. The section is short prose that points at `ROUTER.md`, not the routing logic itself. Every hub has both, and `create-skill` scaffolds them.
26: - The **compiled router** — a precompiled decision table over a hub's `hub-router.json` + `mode-registry.json`, evaluated by a small deterministic engine instead of prose reasoning. It only serves the seven proven hubs in Section 2, is flag-gated (`SPECKIT_COMPILED_ROUTING`) and cohort-gated (`DEFAULT_ON_HUBS`), additive on top of the prose router, and fails closed to it on any gap, error, or ineligible hub.
27: 
28: ### Scope
29: 
30: `create-skill` authors the files the compiled router eventually compiles (`hub-router.json`, `mode-registry.json`, `SKILL.md`) and can mint an onboarding manifest that records a hub's intent to join later. It does not build the compiled engine itself. Sections 5-6 draw that line precisely.
31: 
32: ---
33: 
34: ## 2. WHICH SKILLS THE ROUTER SERVES
35: 
36: The compiled router serves exactly **seven parent hubs**, enumerated as `HUB_CHILD` in `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/014-runtime-engine/lib/compiled-route.cjs`:
37: 
38: | Hub | Shadow-child |
39: | --- | --- |
40: | `sk-code` | `009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code` |
41: | `system-deep-loop` | `009-parent-hub-rollout/002-system-deep-loop` |
42: | `mcp-tooling` | `009-parent-hub-rollout/003-mcp-tooling` |
43: | `cli-external-orchestration` | `009-parent-hub-rollout/004-cli-external-orchestration` |
44: | `cli-classifier` | `009-parent-hub-rollout/008-cli-classifier` |
45: | `sk-doc` | `009-parent-hub-rollout/007-sk-doc` |
46: | `sk-design` | `009-parent-hub-rollout/009-sk-design` |
47: 
48: This same hub set is independently pinned in `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/serving-closure.manifest.json`, the promoted runtime's own inventory of every file the compiled router is allowed to depend on.

97: 1. Writes the hub's final `SKILL.md`, `hub-router.json`, and `mode-registry.json`.
98: 2. Calls `.skilled/bin/compiled-route-manifest.cjs mint` — which compiles those three files through the shared **canonical** compiler (reused from `009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code/lib/registry-compiler.cjs` as a generic reference algorithm, not because the new hub has anything to do with `sk-code`) and, if that compiles cleanly, writes a manifest with `generation: 1`, `servingAuthority: "legacy"`, `shadowOnly: true`.
99: 3. Calls `freshness` against the same inputs and reports `compiled-ready (fresh manifest verified)` only if both steps are valid and hash-fresh. Any failure at either step prints an error, retains the legacy fallback, and never hand-authors a manifest or digest.
100: 
101: What this proves: the hub's own router files are internally self-consistent and compile to a stable hash. What it does **not** do:
102: 
103: | | `--compiled-routing ready` | Genuinely `compiled-serving` |
104: | --- | --- | --- |
105: | Engine | No shadow-child directory exists yet | Hand-built under `009-parent-hub-rollout/00N-<hub>/`, registered in `HUB_CHILD` |
106: | Manifest | `servingAuthority: "legacy"`, `shadowOnly: true` | `servingAuthority: "compiled"`, re-minted to the shadow-child hash |
107: | Coverage proof | None — no scenarios were evaluated | Parity with legacy for the seven admitted hubs; the admission check in Section 4 for a new hub |
108: | Runtime effect | None; the front door always returns the legacy sentinel for this hub | Live, once the hub also joins `DEFAULT_ON_HUBS` (or the flag is forced on) |
109: | Owned by | `create-skill` | The hub's own coverage build-out, then the runtime-engine cohort change (Section 5) |
110: 
111: A freshly minted `ready` manifest is inert onboarding evidence — safe, reversible, and inspectable, but it changes nothing at runtime by itself. Treat `compiled-ready (fresh manifest verified)` as "this hub's files are onboarding-clean," never as "this hub now routes compiled traffic." Standalone skills never touch any of this: the manifest concept, the flag, and the front door are all parent-hub-only.

98: ### Required Standalone Skill Shape
99: 
100: ```text
101: skill-name/
102: ├── SKILL.md
103: ├── ROUTER.md                      # sibling machine router
104: ├── graph-metadata.json
105: ├── leaf-manifest.config.json
106: ├── leaf-scopes.json                # optional: narrows the leaf roots to scopes
107: ├── leaf-manifest.json              # generated
108: ├── leaf-aliases.json               # generated identity projection
109: ├── README.md
110: ├── references/
111: ├── assets/
112: ├── scripts/
113: ├── manual-testing-playbook/          # the scenario corpus — an input
114: │   └── manual-testing-playbook.md    # the index; per-feature files in category folders
115: └── benchmark/                        # what running that corpus produced — output
116:     ├── README.md                     # layout and how to run
117:     └── reports/
118:         ├── README.md                 # run index, appended by the harness
119:         └── <YYYY-MM-DD>--<subject>--<variant>/
120: ```
121: 
122: `SKILL.md` is the root marker. Root JSON requirements are class-specific; the complete authored/generated matrix is [skill-root-metadata-contract.md](references/shared/skill-root-metadata-contract.md). `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/` are optional only when they are genuinely unnecessary.
123: 
124: A standalone skill is class **S** under the root-metadata contract, so beyond `graph-metadata.json` it authors `leaf-manifest.config.json` and generates the rest.
125: That file names its single workflow mode and leaf roots.
126: `leaf-scopes.json` is the optional second authored metadata file: it narrows those roots for the root's single workflow mode, to a subtree or a single doc, when a configured root also holds runtime code or only some of its docs are routable.
127: The generator reads it on both the hub and the standalone path, and falls back to its default walk when it is absent, so a root without one needs no change.
128: A scope must stay under one of the root's declared leaf roots, and the mode it names must be one the root declares, so `OUT_OF_ROOT_LEAF_SCOPE` and `ORPHAN_LEAF_SCOPE_MODE` fail the manifest instead of widening it.
129: Required, forbidden, and generated-versus-authored rules for every root JSON live in [`references/shared/skill-root-metadata-contract.md`](references/shared/skill-root-metadata-contract.md).
130: Do not infer them from a sibling skill.
131: 
132: The last two directories are a pair: `manual-testing-playbook/` holds the corpus a run reads, and
133: `benchmark/` holds what the run wrote. Keeping them apart is what lets a run be re-executed against
134: the same scenarios later and compared, so neither one is optional once a skill is benchmarked.

113: **Objective**: Create skill directory structure with template files.
114: 
115: **Skip only when**: Skill already exists and iteration is needed.
116: 
117: **Command**:
118: ```bash
119: scripts/init_skill.py <skill-name> --path <output-directory>
120: ```
121: 
122: **Required flag**: `--path` names the parent directory the skill folder is created under. The script exits with an error when it is omitted.
123: 
124: **Script Actions**:
125: 1. Creates skill directory at specified path
126: 2. Generates SKILL.md template with proper frontmatter and TODO placeholders
127: 3. Scaffolds `manual-testing-playbook/` and `benchmark/reports/` with their indexes
128: 4. Writes `graph-metadata.json` and `leaf-manifest.config.json`, then runs the class gate to generate `leaf-manifest.json` and `leaf-aliases.json`
129: 
130: **Generated SKILL.md**: `init_skill.py` creates a starter SKILL.md and a sibling `ROUTER.md`. Normalize SKILL.md to the required section order: WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES and REFERENCES.
131: Add recommended sections as the skill needs them. Keep SMART ROUTING to 8 to 12 lines of prose.
132: Put the seeded router pseudocode in `ROUTER.md` under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading, and link to it from SKILL.md.
133: 
134: **After initialization**: Customize or remove generated files as needed.
135: 
136: **Example Usage**:
137: ```bash
138: # Create skill in .skilled/skills/ directory
139: scripts/init_skill.py markdown-optimizer --path .skilled/skills
140: 
141: # Creates:
142: # .skilled/skills/markdown-optimizer/
143: # ├── SKILL.md (with TODO placeholders and a link to ./ROUTER.md)

20: ### What Is a Procedure Card
21: 
22: A procedure card is a private markdown file that adds a repeatable, triggerable PROCESS to an existing skill or mode. It is not a public skill, not a public mode, and does not appear in any advisor routing table. A skill or hub always resolves its public identity first (through its own routing, or a parent hub's `mode-registry.json`). A procedure card is only ever selected AFTER that, from inside the already-chosen skill or mode, by matching the card's own `Trigger` field against the request. A card never grants tool permissions beyond what the owning skill or mode already has.
23: 
24: ### When to Create a Procedure Card
25: 
26: **Create a procedure card when:**
27: - The skill or mode has multiple distinct, individually-triggered internal procedures, not one dominant workflow.
28: - Each procedure needs a strict, lint-able, consistent shape (required fields in a fixed order), not free-form prose.
29: - Fine-grained behavior selection matters, but creating N public skills or modes for what is really one skill or mode with N internal procedures would over-fragment the public surface.
30: - `SKILL.md`'s `HOW IT WORKS` section would otherwise balloon into several near-duplicate workflow write-ups.
31: 
32: **Keep it a plain reference (`skill-reference-template.md`) instead when:**
33: - There is only one dominant workflow, so no selection step is needed.
34: - The content is general background knowledge or context, not an actionable process with its own trigger.
35: - The content always applies whenever the skill or mode runs, rather than only on a specific request shape.
36: 
37: ### Location & Naming
38: 
39: **Standalone skill**: `references/procedures/[procedure-name].md`
40: 
41: **Parent hub, packet-local**: `[packet-name]/procedures/[procedure-name].md`
42: 
43: **Parent hub, cross-packet shared**: `shared/procedures/[procedure-name].md`, only when the procedure genuinely coordinates two or more packets and cannot be owned by one packet without duplicating orchestration.
44: 
45: **Naming Convention**: kebab-case with `.md` extension, same rule as `references/` and `assets/`.
46:

20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Give a person a fast, honest orientation to a skill before they open `SKILL.md`. The README answers what outcome the skill delivers, when to reach for it, what it does not own and how to navigate its files. `SKILL.md` stays the runtime instruction surface. The README is the front door a person reads.
25: 
26: ### Identity Guidance (Purpose First)
27: 
28: The identity of a skill is the outcome it delivers. State that outcome in one plain sentence before naming tools.
29: Describe CLIs, commands, routing paths and reference files only after the outcome.
30: A README that opens with a tool name has not stated its identity.
31: 
32: The mcp-obsidian README states the outcome first: it makes AI use inside Obsidian effective.
33: It names the CLIs and MCP server later as delivery surfaces.
34: Repeat the outcome in the frontmatter description and the pitch.
35: The description supports a quick scan. The pitch opens the full README.
36: 
37: ### Usage
38: 
39: Copy the fillable scaffold in Section 6 into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, then replace every placeholder with current behavior taken from the skill's real files. Keep the numbered ALL-CAPS section headers, the house style and the validator both require them. Drop any section that does not earn its place and renumber the rest.
40: 
41: ### Template Focus
42: 
43: The README gives people a human entry point, current capabilities and a clear route to supporting files. This template provides:
44: 
45: - A one-line pitch in a blockquote right after the H1, stating the outcome before any tool name.
46: - An identity guidance block that puts the delivered outcome ahead of the tooling.
47: - A capability section pattern for a skill's headline strengths, modeled on the pilot's Plugin Knowledge Layer.
48: - A dedicated HVR enforcement section with the banned forms and the scripted checks.
49: - Versioning conventions and a validation checklist that matches the pilot's gates.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 2. SECTION MODEL
54: 
55: A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:
56: 
57: | # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
58: |---|---------|---------|-----------|
59: | 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
60: | 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
61: | 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |
62: | 4 | HOW IT WORKS | The main workflow in prose, with a small Mermaid diagram for multi-step flows | Skill has non-obvious behavior worth explaining |
63: | 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
64: | 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
65: | 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
66: | 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |
67: | 9 | RELATED DOCUMENTS | Stable links out, `SKILL.md` first | Always when links exist |
68: 
69: `OVERVIEW` is the one required section. Its normalized name must appear as a numbered header so the validator finds it. Every other section is optional. A small utility skill might run four sections (AT A GLANCE, OVERVIEW, QUICK START, RELATED DOCUMENTS). A large orchestrator might run all nine. Match the count to the skill. Never pad to hit a number.
70: 
71: Inside OVERVIEW, start with `### What It Does`. Say what the skill is and what the reader gets.
72: Add up to two optional subsections after it.
73: Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to name a current reader problem.
74: Add the capability section below when it earns a table.
75: 
76: ### Capability Section Pattern
77: 
78: When a skill has a headline strength, add a named capability section after What It Does.
79: Use one or two short sentences to say why the strength matters.
80: Use an analogy only when it clarifies the mechanism.
81: Name the section after its domain and add one table row per capability.
82: State the file or data the skill can operate on.
83: Avoid marketing claims. The prose explains why the capability matters. The table states what it does.

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/README.md
-### Why This Skill Exists
-
-Hand-rolling a new skill from a blank `SKILL.md` means reinventing frontmatter rules, section order, routing pseudocode and validation gates every single time. The drift shows up as skills that skip a required field, use the wrong version format, bury routing logic where the advisor can never find it or miss a validation gate entirely. A parent hub multiplies that risk across a registry, a router and however many nested packets, all of which have to agree with each other or the hub silently misroutes. create-skill exists to scaffold both shapes from vetted templates and then prove the result is valid before anyone calls it done.
-
-`init_skill.py` creates `my-skill/` with `SKILL.md` and two prepared trees: a `manual-testing-playbook/` corpus index and a `benchmark/reports/` tree carrying its own run index. `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/` and `scripts/` are added by hand as the skill earns them.
-| Package completion | `python3 scripts/validate_skill_package.py <path>` | Ends with `package_skill.py --check: PASS (exit 0)`. Parent hubs also report legacy or compiled-ready state |
-| Strict contract check | `python3 scripts/validate_skill_package.py <path> --strict` | Promotes noncanonical generated paths from advisory to blocking |
-| Structure extraction | `python3 ../shared/scripts/extract_structure.py <path/to/SKILL.md>` | Prints the parsed section outline for a fast quality read |
-| Leaf-route replay | `node --test .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/tests/leaf-route-replay.test.cjs` | `pass 22` and `fail 0` |
-| [`references/README.md`](./references/README.md) | Route map into the `skill/` and `parent-skill/` reference groups |

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/ROUTER.md
-Requests reach this packet when they ask to create or rebuild an OpenCode skill under `.skilled/skills/`, to run `/create:skill` for a standalone skill or `/create:skill-parent` for a parent hub, to author or repair a skill package's `SKILL.md`, `README.md`, `references/`, `assets/`, `scripts/` or `changelog/`, or to validate and package a skill with `scripts/package_skill.py`. Its vocabulary is `create skill`, `new skill`, `skill scaffold`, `SKILL.md scaffold`, `OpenCode skill`, `parent hub`, `mode packet`, `nested workflow packet` and `package skill`. It routes to two resource families: the `references/shared/` doctrine and its root-metadata contract, which both modes load first, and the mode's own `references/<key>/` plus `assets/<key>/` trees, where `create-skill` resolves the `skill` key and `create-skill-parent` resolves `parent-skill`.

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/assets/parent-skill/parent-skill-hub-template.md
-Packets inside the hub follow the mode-packet shape: a short SMART ROUTING section of 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose, its own `ROUTER.md` beside its `SKILL.md` holding that packet's machine router, and one relative markdown link from the packet's Section 2 to that file. The hub root `ROUTER.md` owns the hub's stage two; each packet's `ROUTER.md` owns the selections that stay inside that packet. See [`skill-md-template.md`](../skill/skill-md-template.md) for the packet `SKILL.md` shape and [`skill-router-template.md`](../skill/skill-router-template.md) for its router file.
-- `ROUTER.md` is the stage-two control document: `router_state: active` declares non-empty equal-key `INTENT_SIGNALS`/`RESOURCE_MAP`, while `router_state: stage1-only` keeps all stage-two collections empty and delegates to stage one. Promote to `active` only after authoring concrete, resolvable leaf paths, never placeholder intents. Its final `## MACHINE ROUTER` section holds the compiled-routing directive and the fallback checklist, so the hub `SKILL.md` never repeats them.

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/references/shared/skill-root-metadata-contract.md
-**Core Principle**: Classify first, then check. A root's class is decided by an authored declaration, never by a generated artifact.
-
-A command surface exists only for hubs that actually ship slash commands, so the file is **optional** for hubs: present (and validated) when the hub owns commands, simply absent when it owns none. Requiring it fleet-wide forced command-less hubs to carry an empty-array placeholder nothing reads, so the rule was reversed to optional — the authority is the class contract module (`scripts/lib/skill-root-metadata-contract.cjs`, where `command-metadata.json` sits in `OPTIONAL_BY_CLASS[CLASS_HUB]`, not the required set), and the standard was set in `sk-doc/019-skill-routing-refactor/021-skill-metadata-json-unification`.
-- **Optional quality block.** `graph-metadata.json` may carry a `quality` object naming the checklists the skill's surface applies. It holds one key, `checklists`, a non-empty array of rows. Each row names its checklist file in `file`, a relative `.md` path inside the skill root, and scopes it with at least one selector: `paths`, `extensions` or `contentMarkers`. Every selector present must be a non-empty array of non-blank strings, and an `extensions` entry must start with a dot. A row carries checklists only, because commands come from the repository's quality config and never from a skill, so any other key at block or row level is refused, `argv`, `command` and `run` included. Every broken rule reports one finding under the quality code in the table below, since the quality runner reads these rows for the files that resolve to the skill's surface, and a block the gate let through would otherwise cover no file, or the wrong one, without a word. A block contributes nothing unless the same file also declares a `surface_detection`, because that surface is what resolves a file to these rows.
-- **Optional signal-provenance lists.** `graph-metadata.json` may carry `intent_signals_generated` and `intent_signals_keep`, each an array of non-blank strings. `generate-router-intent-signals.cjs --write` appends every phrase it adds to `intent_signals_generated`, so an entry there that no router declares any more is an orphan: `--check` reports and counts it, and `--write` removes it from both arrays while keeping the order of what stays. A phrase named in `intent_signals_keep` is left in place, which is how a generated phrase survives a router rename. An `intent_signals` entry no router declares is hand-curated: it never appears in `intent_signals_generated`, so it is never an orphan. A phrase a router does declare is recorded on the hub's first `--write`, so a later router rename prunes it unless `intent_signals_keep` pins it. A present list that holds anything but non-blank strings reports one `GRAPH_METADATA_INVALID_SIGNAL_LIST` finding.
-**A new hub (H):** author `SKILL.md`, `graph-metadata.json`, `description.json`, `mode-registry.json`, and `hub-router.json`, and — only if the hub ships slash commands — `command-metadata.json` (one entry per owned command; omit the file when the hub owns none). Run `--fix` to generate the manifest. Author `leaf-aliases.json` only if a mode genuinely resolves a resource outside its own packet. Add the root `ROUTER.md` stage-two control document per the two-state contract (see [parent-hub-router-schema.md](../parent-skill/parent-hub-router-schema.md)); it is a markdown companion outside the JSON matrix below and does not affect class-H classification.
-Every authored file except `leaf-scopes.json` has a scaffold under `create-skill/assets/`; the two generated files deliberately have none — hand-editing them is what the freshness gate exists to catch. For the scope file, copy the shape from a shipped root.

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/references/shared/validation-and-packaging.md
-**Core Principle**: Validate before you package, and package before you distribute.
-
-- `scripts/quick_validate.py` - minimal frontmatter sanity check
-- `scripts/extract_structure.py` - structure checklist for comprehensive validation
-- `scripts/validate_skill_package.py` - completion gate: classifies the root from its registry/router pair (rejecting a half-declared pair as unclassified), runs the parent-hub root checks, and wraps `package_skill.py --check`; standalone class conformance is enforced by the fleet gate `ci-skill-root-metadata.cjs`
-- `scripts/package_skill.py` - validation plus packaging
-scripts/validate_skill_package.py <path/to/skill>
-**Purpose**: Authoritative pre-completion gate. Run before claiming a skill is done.
-scripts/package_skill.py <path/to/skill> --check
-A machine router block is a fenced block, or an unfenced run of lines such as an indented one, that holds `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`. A fence closes only on a run of the same character at least as long as the one that opened it. A `MACHINE ROUTER` section is an H2 heading that matches `## [N. ]MACHINE ROUTER` outside a fence. The heading alone is the finding, with or without a block below it, so a skill that kept only the prose still fails RS-002. A router block with no section around it reports the same code, because it declares routing in the same file.
-`--strict` promotes all five to errors. Known debt lives in `.skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`, keyed by the skill's path relative to `.skilled/skills` (for example `sk-code/sk-code-review`). A folder outside that root is never debt. Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`, and `machineBlocks` counts the RS-002 findings the entry tolerates, one per leftover section or stray block. A listed skill fails when its line count, word count or number of RS-002 findings grows past the record, or when it shows a code the entry does not record. An entry in any other form is ignored. Remove the entry once the skill is migrated. `/create:skill-parent` applies the same rule as `parent-skill-check.cjs` check `12b-routing-shape`.

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/references/skill/upgrading-a-skill-to-v4.md
-**Core Principle**: Convert a skill into a parent hub only when it has two or more distinct jobs. Keep it single when it has one job. You may also drop the repo's parent `sk-code` and keep your own single skill.
-
-Use existing tooling only. `/create:skill-parent` is the scaffold. `create` will not write on top of an occupied folder (`requires_existing_skill: false`). There is no in-place `--convert` flag here, because converting a skill into a hub is a scaffold-then-move, not an edit. A single skill does convert through `/doctor:sk-skill convert`, in place when it is an older Skilled skill and as a staged new root when it is a plain one, and that command refuses a hub candidate so a skill that really holds two jobs lands here.
-**Convert a single skill in place.** When the skill has one job and is still in a plain shape, or its machine router still sits inside `SKILL.md`, run `/doctor:sk-skill convert <name-or-path>`. It prints the plan first and writes only after your yes. It adds the four-part `version`, writes an `allowed-tools` list only after you approve the list its plan proposes, moves the machine router section verbatim into the sibling `ROUTER.md` and links to it from Smart Routing. A plain skill is staged under its own name as a new root once you approve at least eight intent phrases, and the workflow proves the reshaped prose kept every original body line. The write stops and restores the pre-edit bytes when the parsed router would come out different. Run `/doctor:sk-skill check <name-or-path>` first if you want the gap row by row without any write.

-The compiled skill router is a closed-cohort, byte-verified fast path that resolves a parent hub's `workflowMode` decision without evaluating the hub's prose smart-router at request time. It exists for exactly the parent hubs that have built and proven a compiled policy against that hub's own legacy routing — no other skill, including any hub `create-skill` scaffolds today, is reachable through it. This reference explains what the router actually serves, the chain from a hub's authored files to a live routing decision, the bar a hub must clear to serve compiled traffic, and the exact boundary of `create-skill --compiled-routing ready` — which mints onboarding evidence, not a working compiled route.
-- The **compiled router** — a precompiled decision table over a hub's `hub-router.json` + `mode-registry.json`, evaluated by a small deterministic engine instead of prose reasoning. It only serves the five proven hubs in Section 2, is flag-gated (`SPECKIT_COMPILED_ROUTING`) and cohort-gated (`DEFAULT_ON_HUBS`), additive on top of the prose router, and fails closed to it on any gap, error, or ineligible hub.
-The compiled router serves exactly **five parent hubs**, enumerated as `HUB_CHILD` in `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/014-runtime-engine/lib/compiled-route.cjs`:
-1. **Shadow-child engine** — `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/009-parent-hub-rollout/00N-<hub>/`, holding that hub's own `lib/registry-compiler.cjs` (compiles the hub's `hub-router.json` + `mode-registry.json` + `SKILL.md` into a policy snapshot), `lib/router.cjs` or `lib/canary-router.cjs` (evaluates a prompt against that snapshot), and `fixtures/canary-cases.v1.json` (the hub's own scenario set). Each hub's compiler is hand-built and hand-sized to that hub's real vocabulary — line counts range from 351 (`cli-external-orchestration`) to 698 (`system-deep-loop`); there is no one-size-fits-all compiler.
-Only a `compiled-serving` hub may be added to `DEFAULT_ON_HUBS` — the per-hub cohort the resolver consults when the flag is unset. As of this reference, the five hubs in Section 2 carry that verdict and are in the cohort (verify directly in `014-runtime-engine/lib/resolve.cjs`).
-**This whole path is outside `create-skill`'s authority.** `HUB_CHILD` and `DEFAULT_ON_HUBS` are hardcoded, frozen tables owned by the runtime-engine phase, not derived from any manifest or scaffold output. A hub absent from `HUB_CHILD` always falls back to legacy, by construction, no matter what its manifest says — `create-skill` cannot add a sixth hub to this cohort, and does not attempt to.

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/references/shared/skill-root-metadata-contract.md
-**Core Principle**: Classify first, then check. A root's class is decided by an authored declaration, never by a generated artifact.
-
-A command surface exists only for hubs that actually ship slash commands, so the file is **optional** for hubs: present (and validated) when the hub owns commands, simply absent when it owns none. Requiring it fleet-wide forced command-less hubs to carry an empty-array placeholder nothing reads, so the rule was reversed to optional — the authority is the class contract module (`scripts/lib/skill-root-metadata-contract.cjs`, where `command-metadata.json` sits in `OPTIONAL_BY_CLASS[CLASS_HUB]`, not the required set), and the standard was set in `sk-doc/019-skill-routing-refactor/021-skill-metadata-json-unification`.
-- **Optional quality block.** `graph-metadata.json` may carry a `quality` object naming the checklists the skill's surface applies. It holds one key, `checklists`, a non-empty array of rows. Each row names its checklist file in `file`, a relative `.md` path inside the skill root, and scopes it with at least one selector: `paths`, `extensions` or `contentMarkers`. Every selector present must be a non-empty array of non-blank strings, and an `extensions` entry must start with a dot. A row carries checklists only, because commands come from the repository's quality config and never from a skill, so any other key at block or row level is refused, `argv`, `command` and `run` included. Every broken rule reports one finding under the quality code in the table below, since the quality runner reads these rows for the files that resolve to the skill's surface, and a block the gate let through would otherwise cover no file, or the wrong one, without a word. A block contributes nothing unless the same file also declares a `surface_detection`, because that surface is what resolves a file to these rows.
-- **Optional signal-provenance lists.** `graph-metadata.json` may carry `intent_signals_generated` and `intent_signals_keep`, each an array of non-blank strings. `generate-router-intent-signals.cjs --write` appends every phrase it adds to `intent_signals_generated`, so an entry there that no router declares any more is an orphan: `--check` reports and counts it, and `--write` removes it from both arrays while keeping the order of what stays. A phrase named in `intent_signals_keep` is left in place, which is how a generated phrase survives a router rename. An `intent_signals` entry no router declares is hand-curated: it never appears in `intent_signals_generated`, so it is never an orphan. A phrase a router does declare is recorded on the hub's first `--write`, so a later router rename prunes it unless `intent_signals_keep` pins it. A present list that holds anything but non-blank strings reports one `GRAPH_METADATA_INVALID_SIGNAL_LIST` finding.
-**A new hub (H):** author `SKILL.md`, `graph-metadata.json`, `description.json`, `mode-registry.json`, and `hub-router.json`, and — only if the hub ships slash commands — `command-metadata.json` (one entry per owned command; omit the file when the hub owns none). Run `--fix` to generate the manifest. Author `leaf-aliases.json` only if a mode genuinely resolves a resource outside its own packet. Add the root `ROUTER.md` stage-two control document per the two-state contract (see [parent-hub-router-schema.md](../parent-skill/parent-hub-router-schema.md)); it is a markdown companion outside the JSON matrix below and does not affect class-H classification.
-Every authored file except `leaf-scopes.json` has a scaffold under `create-skill/assets/`; the two generated files deliberately have none — hand-editing them is what the freshness gate exists to catch. For the scope file, copy the shape from a shipped root.

20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines total, with SKILL.md under 1000 lines and the rest in bundled resources (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
